statements.text: AI truly is a game-changing tool, and we need to get the regulation of this tool right, because my staff, for example, asked AI—it might have been GPT-4; it might've been, I don't know, one of the other entities—to create a song that my favorite band, BTS—a song that they would sing somebody else's song, but neither of the artists were involved in creating what sounded like a really genuine song.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI oversight where Senator Hirono illustrates AI capabilities with personal staff experiments before discussing regulation.

statements.text: So, I think that if we're going to go toward a licensing kind of a scheme, we're going to need to put a lot of thought into how we're going to come up with an appropriate scheme that is going to provide the kind of future reference that we need to put in place.
statements.context: Senator Hirono speaks during a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight, questioning witnesses on regulatory approaches.

statements.text: Auto-GPT frightens me. [...] And there are a lot of potential, let's say, cybersecurity risks there. [...] There should be an external agency that says, ``Well, we need to be reassured, if you're going to release this product, that there aren't going to be cybersecurity problems or there are ways of addressing it.''
statements.context: Senator Hirono questions Professor Gary Marcus during a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight.

statements.text: And as we sit here knowing that some entity out there can replicate our voices, put out a campaign ad that we've had nothing to do with, and what are we supposed to do about that? [...] So, the implications are vast on how we should be regulating AI.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI, patents, innovation, and competition.

statements.text: So you're not particularly troubled by the idea that whoever owns the system should own whatever the system generates? [...] I think the owner—I mean, whoever owns the system shouldn't be the dispositive question. [...] the people who use AI as extensions of their minds should be the inventors.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI and IP, Part I: Patents, Innovation, and Competition.

statements.text: So is your position that every artist's work before it can be used to train AI models, that the company that is wanting to use that information has got to get the consent of the originator?
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property, Part II: Copyright.

statements.text: So do you know if—well, I think you mentioned that your work has been used to train AI models and you have gotten not one cent for that use.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property, Part II: Copyright.

statements.text: And you think that we are able to do this knowing that these platforms incorporate billions and billions of information to train their AI models?
statements.context: Senate hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property, Part II: Copyright.

statements.text: So how can we use AI or other tools to rapidly detect and counter such efforts to spread disinformation, especially in emergencies or following disasters?
statements.context: Senate hearing questioning Department of Energy witnesses on AI's role in countering disaster-related disinformation.

statements.text: For Dr. Stevens, in the wake of the devastating fire on Maui, residents have been subject to disinformation on social media, likely coordinated by foreign governments, governmental entities, and generated with AI to discourage residents from reaching out to FEMA for disaster assistance and to sow distrust in the Federal Government.
statements.context: Senate hearing questioning a witness on AI-generated disinformation following the Maui wildfires.

statements.text: So every time we have one of these hearings, we learn something new. But the conclusion I've drawn is that AI is ubiquitous. Anybody can use AI. It can be used in any endeavor. So when I hear you folks testifying about how we shouldn't be taking half measures, I'm not sure what that means.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI oversight where Senator Hirono questions a witness about the appropriate scope of AI regulation.

statements.text: And that happened during the disaster on Maui. And Maui residents were subject to disinformation, some of it coming from foreign governments, i.e., Russia, looking to sow confusion and distress, including, ``Don't sign up for FEMA because they cannot be trusted.''
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight, Senator Hirono questioning a witness about AI-enabled disinformation during disasters.

statements.text: [...] one of the concerns about AI from the worker standpoint is that their jobs will be gone. [...] Professor Hartzog, you mentioned that [...] generative AI can result in job losses. [...] what are the kinds of jobs that will be lost to AI?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'Oversight of A.I.: Legislating on Artificial Intelligence', Senator Hirono questioning expert witnesses.

statements.text: it just seems to make sense that the creators of the content should get some kind of compensation for the use of their material in training the AI platforms.
statements.context: Senator Hirono poses questions during a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight and the future of journalism.

statements.text: do you think that current law, the application of current law should sort of be left and determined by what cases, lawsuits that have been filed? How do we clarify that current law applies in the AI situation?
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI and the future of journalism, questioning a witness.

statements.text: The use of AI, I think, is going to be very prevalent in this election, upcoming election season. The voters should know that they will be subjected—they may not know it. They may not even believe that it's happening to them.
statements.context: Senate oversight hearing on AI-generated election deepfakes, Senator Hirono questioning a witness about voter awareness of AI-generated political disinformation.

statements.text: But where does educating the public come into play, to let them know that, as we are approaching or we're already in an election situation, that they should expect to experience AI-created audio, video fake stuff, that—where does educating the public to the fact that they will be subjected to all of this come into play, to inoculate them against the impact of this kind of fake, deepfake material?
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on oversight of AI and election deepfakes.

statements.text: are you also resorting to AI and other means of making your intel collection more efficient and effective, because there is a huge need for people with this kind of background, but we do not have those people yet? [...] On the artificial intelligence question about how do we become more efficient, I think what you will find across the Intelligence Community is that we are applying AI, and in closed session we can also talk about counter-AI.
statements.context: Senate hearing on worldwide threats, Senator Hirono questioning General Kruse on intelligence workforce shortages and AI adoption in the Defense Intelligence Community.
